title: Small experiments, better questions
excerpt: An experiment does not need to become a product to be useful. Start with a question, set a boundary, and make the result easy to learn from.
content:
## Start with the uncertainty

“We should build a prototype” sounds like a plan. But a prototype is only useful when it helps answer a question. Before choosing a tool or sketching an interface, write down what you do not yet understand.

For example: *Can someone understand the result without an explanation?* That question suggests a very different experiment from *Can the system respond quickly enough?*

## Give the experiment a boundary

Choose one thing to learn and a small amount of work that could reveal it. The boundary is part of the design. It keeps an experiment from quietly turning into a full product before its assumptions have been tested.

1. State the question.
2. Describe an observable signal.
3. Build the smallest experience that produces that signal.
4. Record what happened, including surprises.

> An experiment earns its keep when it changes the next decision.

## Keep a decision log

A short note is enough. Write down the assumption, the observation, and the next action. Keep observations separate from interpretations: “three people missed the control” is different from “the layout is confusing.”

That distinction makes the result easier to revisit. A future version of the team can understand the evidence without inheriting every conclusion.

## Leave room to stop

Sometimes the best result is deciding not to continue. An experiment that exposes an unhelpful premise has still done useful work. Keep the lesson, preserve a small example if it helps, and carry the question into the next attempt.
